solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Delightful lake in rustic surroundings

indicators.note: 'in ... surroundings' says one piece sits inside the country word that is wrapped around it

blocks.note: a rustic is a country labourer
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A charming lake set among unspoilt countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rustic' looks like an adjective describing the surroundings, but here it is a noun for a country person, and L goes inside: PE-L-ASANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasant and delightful are near-synonyms, both meaning agreeable and enjoyable.

clue.text: Expose what nudists did on beach?

blocks.note: first meaning: to reveal or uncover
second, playful meaning: people with no clothes stretched out naked on the sand

explanation.surface: A sly question about what goes on at a naturist beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic, flagged by the question mark: read literally, the phrase says nudists lay there bare.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something bare is an idiom for revealing it fully, which is to expose it.

clue.text: Some in LA mourned this secret love affair

indicators.note: 'some in' says only a part of the following words is wanted, sitting within them

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: People in Los Angeles grieved over a clandestine romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Amour, borrowed from French, is a love affair, especially an illicit or hidden one.

clue.text: Man, not married, drinking this in boozer?

indicators.note: 'not married' tells you to take away the abbreviation for married from the word before

blocks.note: a man is a male
M is the standard abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A single man having a drink at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A boozer is British slang for a pub. The definition is by example, hence the question mark: what you might be drinking there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale is a type of beer, the typical drink served in a British pub.

clue.text: Teens seen running wild in US state

indicators.note: something running wild is out of control and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Teenagers spotted rampaging somewhere in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennessee is one of the fifty American states, home of Nashville and Memphis.

clue.text: Old-time chap from Scotland chosen, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what you said points to how the word is heard rather than written

blocks.note: chosen means picked

explanation.surface: Asking whether an ancient Scottish man was the one selected.
explanation.definitionFit: The Picts were an ancient people of northern and eastern Scotland, so one of them is an old-time Scot.

clue.text: Everyone steering clear of this drug den

blocks.note: pot is slang for cannabis
a hole is a squalid den or hideaway

explanation.surface: People avoiding a place where drugs are taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drug den' reads as one phrase, but it splits into two pieces; the definition is a description of a road hazard drivers swerve around.
explanation.definitionFit: A pothole is a hollow in a road surface, which all motorists try to steer around.

clue.text: Took refuge in church, getting rebuke

indicators.note: 'in' places the refuge word inside the church abbreviation

blocks.note: CE stands for the Church of England
to take refuge is to hide

explanation.surface: Someone sheltered in a church and was told off for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To chide is to scold or reprove, the same as to rebuke.

clue.text: Choose to make U-turn, concealing company's last mistake

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the word is read backwards
to conceal is to hide inside, so the turned word wraps around another piece
'last' keeps only the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: to choose is to opt
the final letter of company

explanation.surface: Deciding to turn back to hide a firm's latest blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A typo is a slip in typing or printing, a small textual mistake.

clue.text: A German mug? On the contrary

definitions.text: A German mug? On the contrary

blocks.note: ein is German for a
a stein is a large beer mug

explanation.surface: Is that German a fool? Quite the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue describes a German who is anything but a mug, that is, a fool: the opposite of a mug is a genius.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, the German-born physicist, is the byword for a genius, the opposite of a gullible fool.

clue.text: Coach's posture

blocks.note: first meaning: a railway passenger vehicle
second meaning: the way a person holds their body

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it look like a sports coach's stance; it is really two separate meanings joined by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A carriage is a railway coach, and also the bearing or deportment of a person.

clue.text: Your share of vegetable patch?

blocks.note: first meaning: the portion allotted to you
second meaning: a rented plot for growing produce

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an allotment is a small plot of council land rented for growing vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is both an apportioned share and a rented garden plot used for growing crops.

clue.text: Sign submarine captain will return

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the captain's name is read backwards

blocks.note: Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne's novel

explanation.surface: An augury that a submarine's commander is coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a portent or sign of what is to come.

clue.text: Women I allowed to retain a servant

indicators.note: to retain is to hold onto, so the words keep the answer inside them

blocks.note: a run of letters across the three words

explanation.surface: A woman was permitted to keep a domestic helper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'allowed to' reads as permission, but 'to retain' is the signal for letters held within the words before.
explanation.definitionFit: A menial is a domestic servant, especially one doing lowly work.

clue.text: Test cricket perhaps absorbing papa

indicators.note: absorbing means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a cricket is an example of an insect
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Test match in cricket that soaks up Dad's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test cricket' looks like one phrase about an international match; split it so Test is the definition and cricket is the chirping creature.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect is to examine closely, which is to test or check something.

clue.text: Drawing of small boat

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: A picture of a little boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A sketch is a rough drawing made quickly.

clue.text: Vehicle about to go over animal's remains

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
C stands for circa, Latin for about
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A vehicle about to run over the body of a dead animal.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'go over' means sit on top, so the abbreviation for about stands above the animal; 'animal's remains' reads as one phrase, but the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A carcass is the dead body of an animal, its remains.

clue.text: No Rolling Stone will have such a hanger-on

definitions.text: No Rolling Stone will have such a hanger-on

blocks.note: surface reading: no member of the rock band would put up with a groupie or hanger-on
setter's reading: the proverb says a rolling stone gathers no plant growth, so a stone that keeps moving never has this clinging to it

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals suggest Mick Jagger's band; the clue really rests on the proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no ...', and the hanger-on is a plant that clings to stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Moss is a small plant that grows clinging to stones, gathering only on those that stay still.

clue.text: Hold forth in Old English about traitor

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the language abbreviation wraps the traitor word

blocks.note: OE is the standard abbreviation for Old English
a rat is a traitor or informer

explanation.surface: Someone sounding off in archaic language about a betrayer.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak pompously at length, the same as to hold forth.

clue.text: Remedy almost certain to produce riches

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the remedy word is dropped

blocks.note: to remedy an ailment is to treat it
certain means sure

explanation.surface: A cure that is all but guaranteed to make a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasure is a store of wealth or valuables, which is to say riches.

clue.text: Wretched chap, one interrupting news broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so these letters are scattered into a new order
something interrupting breaks into the middle, so it goes inside the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A miserable man cutting into a news bulletin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news broadcast' looks like a TV bulletin, but broadcast here means scattered, the old farming sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Swine is an insult for a contemptible or nasty person, a wretched fellow.

clue.text: Obscure travelling salesmen

indicators.note: travelling means moving about, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Unknown sales reps on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travelling salesmen' is a stock phrase, which hides that travelling is the signal and Obscure the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An obscure person is unknown or unremarked, so without a name anyone recognises.

clue.text: Outspoken Pole in Bath perhaps

indicators.note: outspoken means said out loud, so the word for pole is heard rather than written

blocks.note: a pole, such as a ship's mast or boom

explanation.surface: A frank Polish person visiting an English city.
explanation.walkthrough: Pole looks like a nationality; it is a length of wood. In British speech the final R is silent. Bath is an English city famous for its Roman hot springs.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath is an example of a spa town, a place with mineral springs where people take the waters.

clue.text: Country I was the leader of

blocks.note: taken as written
to lead an organisation is to run it

explanation.surface: A former ruler boasting about the nation they governed.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation in western Asia, formerly known as Persia.

clue.text: As drunk as this, went mad?

indicators.note: mad means crazy and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Was someone so inebriated they lost their mind?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed as a newt' is a British idiom for very drunk; the definition asks for the creature in that comparison.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'drunk as a newt' compares an extremely intoxicated person to this small amphibian.

clue.text: Revolutionary art and poetry making you cross

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round, so the word art is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
poetry is verse

explanation.surface: Radical paintings and poems that leave you angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like the adjective for angry, but it is the verb meaning to go across.
explanation.definitionFit: To traverse is to travel across or over, so it is a synonym of cross as a verb.
